title: Living because of death
hook: because life is short, love now
tomorrow: what can you know for sure about death, and what can't you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, fear of death, and its four roots: wanting, the body, regret and doubt. Meet the fear. Then a question: if life is this short, what comes first?

A funeral ends, and the cousins' group chat goes quiet for a day. Then someone types: love you guys. Everyone answers within the hour, even the uncle who never texts. So, what comes first when life is short? An old verse answers, and it isn't a bucket list. It's: stop the fight. But it hides that answer in an odd spot. Why is a verse about dying sitting in the middle of a pair about grudges?
screen: `LOVE YOU GUYS.` → `NOT A BUCKET LIST.` → `WHY IS DEATH IN A VERSE ABOUT GRUDGES?`

segments.voice: Open the Dhammapada, the old collection of the Buddha's verses, near the start. Verse five, in Max Müller's translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." A verse about fighting. Then verse six: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." So why does death show up in a lesson about grudges? Here's the solve. Every quarrel quietly assumes time. Time to be right later. Time to make up next month. Time for them to come around first. Knowing that we all come to an end takes that borrowed time away, and the quarrel loses the floor it was standing on. Death isn't the gloomy part of the verse. It's the reason the fighting stops. That's living because of death: the shortness of life isn't a threat hanging over love; it's the push toward it. And one detail worth passing on tonight: Max Müller's word love stands for a Pali word that more literally means non-hatred. The verse doesn't demand a giant feeling. It asks you to set the hatred down. Love now doesn't have to be a speech. It can be a short message, sent while there's still a today to send it in.
screen: `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `WE MUST ALL COME TO AN END HERE.` · `EVERY QUARREL ASSUMES TIME.` · `NON-HATRED, NOT A GIANT FEELING.` · then, large: `LOVE NOW.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind who hasn't heard it from you lately. In your head, or on your phone without sending yet, find the words you'd actually use: love you, or thank you, or I'm glad you're here. Then rest with their face in mind, breathing easily, until the words feel like yours.
Living because of death: letting the shortness of life push you toward love instead of away from it. In the Dhammapada, knowing we all come to an end is what ends the quarrel.
Pocket this: love now, not someday, not once the moment is perfect. One day left in this block.

original.note: Pali: non-hatred, non-enmity. In verse 5, 'hatred ceases by averena', which Max Müller renders 'by love'.

notes: Quotations from Max Müller's Dhammapada (SBE vol. 10, 1881), verses 5 and 6; confirm punctuation (the 1881 text uses dashes) word for word.
'Love' in verse 5 renders Pali averena (by non-hatred / non-enmity); confirm phrasing 'more literally means non-hatred'.

Verse 6's Pali (yamamase) is read by some translators as 'we come to an end' and by others as 'we must restrain ourselves'; the trapdoor says only that translators read it in more than one way. Confirm.
Puzzle shape: the odd detail is a death verse paired with a hatred verse; the solve is 'every quarrel assumes time'. That reading is the script's framing, not a commentary's; confirm it's fair.
